references.text: The context for the gold plate with the inscription 'Holy to the Lord' that is to be attached to the turban and worn on Aaron's forehead.
The priests bear the guilt of the people and make atonement for them before the Lord.
Warning about bearing guilt by profaning the holy offerings.
Aaron and his sons shall bear the guilt associated with the sanctuary and the priesthood.
The suffering servant bears the sins of many, a prophetic parallel to the high priest who bears the people's guilt.
High Priest Joshua is given a clean turban placed on his head, a symbol of purity and forgiveness.
Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, fulfilling the high priest's role in bearing guilt.
Christ bore our sins in his body on the cross, the ultimate fulfillment of bearing the people's guilt.
Jesus as a merciful and faithful high priest makes atonement for the people's sins.
Christ as eternal high priest intercedes and does not need to offer sacrifices daily like the Levitical priests.
Complementary functions for Aaron as mediator: the shoulders bear the names as a reminder, the forehead bears the guilt for holy offerings.
Complementary description of the priest's mediatorial role: the breastplate (heart/remembrance) and the forehead (guilt/acceptance).
Close connection between bearing judgment (Urim and Thummim) and bearing guilt; both are necessary aspects of the priest's service.
Theological parallel between continuously bearing guilt (forehead) and ritual removal of sins (scapegoat).
Complementary responsibility: Aaron receives the offerings (v. 9) but also bears their guilt (v. 38).
